get_config.description: Fetch the full config: activities and devices, each with a label and numeric id, plus each device's controlGroup command lists (the names send_command takes).

returns.description: Activities: {id, label, type, ...}; id "-1" is PowerOff.
returns.name: data.activity[]

get_current_activity.description: Which activity is running; data.result is the activity id as a string, "-1" when everything is off.

get_provision_info.description: Fetch the hub's remoteId, the value every WebSocket frame's hubId and the connect path carry. One HTTP POST on port 8088 -- the same port as the socket -- with the Origin header the hub insists on. Not authenticated; any LAN client may call it.

returns.description: The remoteId; store it as the `remote_id` credential.
returns.name: data.activeRemoteId

power_off.description: Stop the current activity: runactivity with the built-in PowerOff activity, id -1.

send_command.description: Press a single device command (e.g. VolumeUp) on a device by id -- the PRESS half of a key. Follow it with send_command_release, ~100 ms later, or the hub treats the key as held. The `action` argument is a JSON-looking STRING with every colon doubled ("::"), exactly as the hub wants it (hub_protocol.hold_action).
send_command.example_notes: Worked case: VolumeUp on device 12345. The inner action value is a string, so its quotes are escaped in the frame.

command.description: Command name from the device's controlGroup function list in get_config (e.g. VolumeUp, Mute, PowerToggle).

send_command_release.description: The RELEASE half of send_command: identical frame with status "release". Send it after every press; the gap between the two is the hold duration.
send_command_release.example_notes: Worked case: the release matching the send_command example.

command.description: The same command name the press carried.

start_activity.description: Start an activity by its id (turns on and switches inputs across the AV stack). The hub streams code-100 progress frames until the activity is up.

activity_id.description: Activity id from get_config (data.activity[].id), as a string; -1 is the built-in PowerOff activity.

methods.notes: Hubs answer SSDP for urn:myharmony-com:device:harmony:1 (this is the search target Home Assistant's discovery uses). The community harmonyhubjs-discover tool alternatively listens on a local UDP port for hub responses.

device.name: Logitech Harmony Hub
device.notes:
The Harmony Hub is Logitech's IR/Bluetooth/IP universal-remote bridge: it holds a configuration of "activities" (Watch TV, Play Game) and "devices" and blasts IR / sends IP or Bluetooth commands to control an AV stack. Logitech ended Harmony manufacturing in April 2021 and has begun dropping support for older remotes, so the hardware is on borrowed time — but local control survives entirely without Logitech's cloud.
LOCAL CONTROL: the hub exposes a WebSocket API on TCP 8088 with no authentication beyond a locally-retrievable `remoteId`. A one-time HTTP POST to port 8088 returns the remoteId; the client then opens a WebSocket and issues JSON requests: get the config (activities + devices, each with a label and id), get the current activity, start/stop an activity by id, send a device command, hold a command for a duration, and change channel. Every request carries a unique id echoed in the reply. Idle WebSocket connections are closed by the hub after ~60s unless pinged.
HISTORY (worth knowing): firmware 4.15.206 (Dec 2018) removed the older XMPP local API and broke local control; after community backlash Logitech restored a local API path (XMPP re-enabled in 4.15.250, Feb 2019) and committed to keeping local access. Modern firmware defaults to the WebSocket transport; legacy hubs may still expose XMPP. aioharmony speaks both.

openness.notes: Logitech publishes no local protocol documentation; the WebSocket and XMPP surfaces were reverse-engineered by the community. aioharmony (which Home Assistant uses) is the reference implementation.

issued_to_client: remoteId (retrieved from the hub over the port-8088 POST; gates the WebSocket session)
credentials.notes: The remoteId is retrievable by any LAN client — it is not a secret so much as a session parameter. Local control is otherwise unauthenticated on the LAN. The Wi-Fi passphrase is handled by the app, not the control API documented here.

factory_reset.effect: Resets the hub to unconfigured state (clears Wi-Fi and the activity/ device configuration). Performed from the Harmony app or a hardware reset; the exact procedure is model/firmware specific and not transcribed here.

procedures.basis: Logitech support documents an in-app reset; not replayed here.
procedures.name: Reset from the Harmony app

steps.action: Use the Harmony app's reset option (or the documented power-cycle) to return the hub to setup.
steps.expect: The hub reboots into unconfigured/setup state.

cloud.local_alternative: Yes for CONTROL — once the hub is configured, the local WebSocket API on port 8088 drives it with no cloud. Editing the activity/device configuration, however, has historically required the Harmony app; with Logitech's servers winding down, export/keep a working configuration while it can still be authored.

methods.description: Activity/device configuration is authored in the Harmony app, which historically synced with the MyHarmony cloud. After configuration, control is fully local (see the WebSocket API); no account is needed at control time.

remote_id.notes: The value the WebSocket connect path's `{remote_id}` and every frame's `hubId` are filled from. Not a secret -- any LAN client can fetch it again -- but it is per-hub, so store it keyed by the hub's UDN.

steps.action: Configure activities and devices in the Harmony app (one-time, cloud-assisted).
Retrieve the hub's remoteId with the port-8088 provisioning POST (`get_provision_info`), then open the WebSocket for local control.
steps.expect: JSON reply whose data.activeRemoteId is the hub's remoteId.

setup.notes: A hub's activities and devices are configured through Logitech's app (historically backed by the MyHarmony cloud database). Once configured, local control needs no pairing: any LAN client fetches the remoteId with the port-8088 POST below and opens the WebSocket. Initial Wi-Fi onboarding is app-driven and not documented here.

rejoin.notes: Wi-Fi can be reconfigured from the app while the hub is reachable. Local control resumes once the hub rejoins the LAN.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. Facts are from the aioharmony and harmonyhub-api open-source clients and Home Assistant's integration; the WebSocket envelope, command strings and params in `websocket`/`commands` were transcribed from aioharmony's source (hubconnector_websocket.py, const.py, harmonyclient.py) rather than captured, so they are `reported`.

http_endpoints.description: One-time handshake on port 8088. POST with headers Origin: http://sl.dhg.myharmony.com, Content-Type: application/json, Accept-Charset: utf-8, and body {"id":1,"cmd":"setup.account?getProvisionInfo","params":{}}. The reply carries the hub's remoteId, which the WebSocket session below needs.
http_endpoints.name: Provisioning — get remoteId (port 8088)

fields.description: The hub's remoteId (per-hub, not a session credential); fills `{remote_id}` in the WebSocket connect path and every frame's `hubId`.
fields.name: data.activeRemoteId

hub_protocol.activities: runactivity takes params {"async":"true","timestamp":0,"activityId": "<id>"}; the hub streams progress frames (code 100, data.done / data.total) and pushes an "activityId" change notification when the activity is running. Activity id "-1" is the built-in PowerOff. The current activity is getCurrentActivity, whose data.result is the id.
hub_protocol.envelope: Every request on the socket is one JSON text frame {"hubId": "<remoteId>", "timeout": <seconds>, "hbus": {"cmd": "<mime>?<operation>", "id": <client-chosen unique id>, "params": {...}}}. The hub answers with a frame carrying the same id, a "code" (100 = in progress, 200 = done) and "data". cmd is the pair of an XMPP-era mime type and an operation, joined with "?": "vnd.logitech.harmony/vnd.logitech.harmony.engine?config", "harmony.activityengine?runactivity", "vnd.logitech.harmony/vnd.logitech.harmony.engine?holdAction". The `timeout` is the hub-side reply timeout in seconds (aioharmony sends 5, the Node clients 30; either works). Reads take params {"verb":"get","format":"json"}.
hub_protocol.history: Firmware 4.15.206 (Dec 2018) removed the XMPP local API on TCP 5222; 4.15.250 (Feb 2019) restored it after community backlash. The WebSocket surface above is the one modern firmware speaks by default; aioharmony keeps an XMPP connector for hubs that still expose 5222. Only the WebSocket transport is declared here.
hub_protocol.hold_action: A device command is a press followed by a release: two holdAction frames whose params differ only in "status" ("press", then "release"). The "action" param is a STRING, not an object, and inside it every colon is doubled -- {"command":: "VolumeUp","type":: "IRCommand","deviceId":: "12345"} -- which is the hub's own escaping of the XMPP-era attribute syntax (PROTOCOL.md shows the same "::" in the XMPP form). Send the release a short interval after the press (aioharmony defaults to ~0.1 s; a longer gap is a held key).
hub_protocol.keepalive: Idle sockets are closed by the hub after ~60 s; aioharmony sends a WebSocket ping every 30 s and expects a pong within 15 s.
hub_protocol.provisioning: Before the socket can be opened the client needs the hub's remoteId: POST http://<ip>:8088/ with Origin: http://sl.dhg.myharmony.com, Content-Type: application/json, Accept: application/json and Accept-Charset: utf-8, body {"id":1,"cmd":"setup.account?getProvisionInfo","params":{}}. The reply is {"cmd":..., "code":200, "data":{"activeRemoteId": "<remoteId>", ...}}. The Origin header is what the hub keys the request on; without it the POST is refused.
hub_protocol.transport: WebSocket, JSON text frames, TCP 8088; provisioning over HTTP on the same port

channels.description: The only channel. Every request is one JSON text frame in this envelope; replies carry the same id with "code" and "data" (hub_protocol.envelope). The hub also pushes unsolicited frames on this socket (activity changes, config updates) with no request id.
channels.name: hbus

websocket.notes: No pairing block: the socket needs nothing beyond the remoteId in the connect path, and that is fetched from the hub itself by get_provision_info -- not issued by a consent flow the schema's pairing modes describe. Verification: reported (aioharmony, harmonyhubjs).
